The quotient rule. A fundamental formula for differentiating ratios of two functions. If h of x equals f of x divided by g of x, where g of x is not equal to zero, then the derivative h prime of x equals the quantity f prime of x times g of x minus f of x times g prime of x, all divided by g of x squared. The quotient rule is one of the foundational differentiation techniques alongside the power rule, product rule, and chain rule. While it can be derived from the product and chain rules, the quotient rule is so common—rational functions are ubiquitous—that it is typically memorized and applied directly. A helpful memory aid is "low d-high minus high d-low, over low-low." The denominator is squared, and the numerator is the derivative of the numerator times the denominator minus the numerator times the derivative of the denominator. The quotient rule can be derived from the product rule applied to f of x times one divided by g of x, combined with the chain rule for the reciprocal. When you apply the quotient rule to rational functions—polynomials divided by polynomials—the result is another rational function. The derivative is undefined where g of x equals zero, which are the discontinuities and vertical asymptotes of the original function. Let me work through an example. The derivative of x squared divided by the quantity x plus one equals the quantity two x times the quantity x plus one minus x squared times one, all divided by the quantity x plus one squared. This simplifies to two x squared plus two x minus x squared, all divided by x plus one squared, which further simplifies to x squared plus two x, all divided by x plus one squared. The quotient rule is used for derivatives of tangent of x, which equals sine of x divided by cosine of x, and for logarithm base a of x, which equals the natural logarithm of x divided by the natural logarithm of a. A special case is the reciprocal rule: if h of x equals one divided by g of x, then h prime of x equals negative g prime of x divided by g of x squared. This is a simplified quotient rule where f of x equals one. The quotient rule is one of a trinity of basic differentiation techniques that enables differentiation of all elementary functions. While not as universally applicable as the chain rule, it is indispensable for rational functions, which appear everywhere in control theory, signal processing, and physics. Differentiation rules are compositional—complex derivatives are built from simpler rules applied layer by layer. In numerical differentiation, finite-difference approximations to quotient-rule formulas are used to estimate derivatives computationally.
